:::{#def-projection-matrix}
#### Orthogonal projection matrix

A square matrix $\matr{P}$ is an **orthogonal projection matrix**
if it is both symmetric (@def-symmetric-matrix)
and idempotent (@def-idempotent-matrix):

$$\tp{\matr{P}} = \matr{P}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\matr{P}^2 = \matr{P}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-oblique-projection}
#### Oblique projection

A square matrix is an **oblique projection**
if it is idempotent (@def-idempotent-matrix)
but not symmetric (@def-symmetric-matrix).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-projection-matrix}
#### An orthogonal projection and an oblique one

$\matr{P} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
is symmetric, and $\matr{P}^2 = \matr{P}$,
so $\matr{P}$ is an orthogonal projection matrix;
it maps $(v_1, v_2)$ to $(v_1, 0)$.

$\matr{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
is idempotent:

$$
\matr{Q}^2
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 0 & 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 0 \\ 0 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0 & 0 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
= \matr{Q},
$$

but $\tp{\matr{Q}} \neq \matr{Q}$,
so $\matr{Q}$ is an oblique projection,
not an orthogonal projection matrix.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-projection-matrix-terminology}
#### What "projection matrix" means in these notes

Some texts call any idempotent matrix a projection matrix,
so that both $\matr{P}$ and $\matr{Q}$ in @exm-projection-matrix
would count as one.
Regression texts often say "projection matrix"
when they mean an orthogonal one.
In these notes, "projection matrix" always means
an orthogonal projection matrix in the sense of @def-projection-matrix,
such as $\matr{P}$ in @exm-projection-matrix,
and never an oblique projection (@def-oblique-projection)
such as $\matr{Q}$.

:::
